Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 113, verses 1–5:

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. The meaning of "a'udhu" (I seek refuge) has already been explained in the discussion of seeking refuge (al-ta'awwudh), and the meaning of "rabb" (Lord) in the languages and in al-Fatiha. As for "al-falaq" (the daybreak), there are three opinions. The first: it is the dawn, from the phrase "faliq al-isbah" (the cleaver of the morning). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). The second: it is everything that God cleaves, such as the earth splitting to bring forth plants, mountains splitting to release springs, clouds splitting to release rain, wombs splitting to bring forth offspring, grains and date-pits, and other things. The third: it is a pit in Hell. This has been related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾. This is general over all created beings, and their evil takes many forms, from which God protect us. "Ma" here may be a relative pronoun (mawsulah), a descriptive (mawsufah), or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. On this there are seven opinions. The first: it is the night when it grows dark, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿until the darkening of the night﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. This is the view of most scholars. The darkness of night is when the people of evil, among mankind and jinn, spread out, and for this reason it is said in the proverb: "The night is more concealing for mischief." The second: it is the moon. Al-Nasai related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: "O Aisha, seek refuge in God from the evil of this, for it is the darkness when it settles." Its settling here means its eclipse, because "waqab" in the speech of the Arabs means darkness and blackness, and also means entering; so the meaning is when it enters into eclipse or when it becomes dark by it. The third: it is the sun when it sets, and "al-waqub" on this meaning is darkness or entering. The fourth: the darkness is the day when it enters the night, which is close to the preceding. The fifth: the darkness is the setting of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and diseases and plague would rise up at it. It has been related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The star is the darkness," so it may be that he meant the Pleiades. The sixth: al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the darkness" is meant the black snake, and its "settling" is its striking. The seventh: it is Iblis, related by al-Suhayli.

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. "Al-nafth" resembles blowing without spittle and saliva, as said by Ibn Atiyya, while al-Zamakhshari said it is blowing with saliva. This "nafth" is a kind of magic: that one blows over knots tied in a thread or the like, over the name of the person bewitched, so that it harms him. Ibn Atiyya related that a trustworthy person told him that he saw, among some people in the desert of the Maghrib, a red thread in which knots had been tied over young camels, which prevented them from suckling their mothers; whenever a knot was untied, that young camel would run to its mother and suckle at once. Al-Zamakhshari said: in seeking refuge from "the blowers" there are three aspects: first, that one seeks refuge from the likes of their deed, which is magic, for those who practise it. Second, that one seeks refuge from their deceit of people and their temptation. Third, that one seeks refuge from the evil that befalls by their blowing. "Al-naffathat" is an intensive form, and the qualified noun is omitted; its estimate is: the women who blow, or the group who blow, or the souls that blow. The first is more correct, because it has been related that it refers to the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam the Jew, who were sorceresses; they and their father bewitched the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and tied for him eleven knots, so God sent down the two refuges, eleven verses corresponding to the number of knots, and God healed His Messenger (ﷺ). If it is asked: why was "the blowers" defined with the article (al-), while what precedes it, "darkness", and what follows it, "envier", were indefinite, although all are things sought refuge from? The answer: the blowers were defined to indicate generality, since every blower is evil, unlike the darkness and the envier, whose evil is in some cases but not others.

﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. Envy is a blameworthy disposition, by nature and by the law. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Envy devours good deeds as fire devours firewood." Some scholars said: envy was the first sin by which God was disobeyed in heaven and on earth. In heaven, it was the envy of Iblis toward Adam; on earth, it was the killing of Hābīl by his brother Qābīl because of envy. Then envy has degrees. The first: that a person loves the removal of a blessing from his Muslim brother, even if it would not pass to him, rather he dislikes God's bounty upon another and is pained by it. The second: that he loves the removal of that blessing because he desires it and its transfer to himself. The third: that he wishes for himself the like of that blessing without loving its removal from others; this is permissible and is not envy, but rather is "ghibta" (emulation). The envier harms himself in three ways. First: the acquisition of sins, because envy is forbidden. Second: bad manners with God the Exalted, for the reality of envy is hatred of God's bestowal upon His servant and an objection to God in His action. Third: the heart's pain from its constant worry and grief. So we ask God to make us envied, not envious, for the envied is in blessing and the envier is in distress and affliction. And how well the one who said:

"Indeed I pity my envious ones, for the excess of what their breasts hold of rancour,
They look at God's dealings with me, so their eyes are in Paradise while their hearts are in Fire."

Another said:

"If they envy me, I do not blame them, for before me the people of virtue were envied too,
So may there remain for me and for them what is with me and with them, and may most of us die of the rage at what he finds."

Then the envier's enmity never ceases, and his appeasement is of no use; he is a wrongdoer who complains as if he were wronged. And how true is the one who said:

"Every enmity may hope to have its removal, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy."

And the wisest of poets said:

"And the most wrongful of God's creatures is one who spends the night envious
Of one who spends the night turning in his blessings."

Ibn Atiyya said: some of the skilled scholars said: this surah is five verses, and it is what people mean by their saying to an envier from whom one fears the evil eye: "The five on your eye." If it is asked: why was it qualified with "when it settles" and "when he envies", with "idha", which implies the restriction of some times? The answer: the evil of the envier and his harm only occur when he carries out his envy; then he harms by his speech, by his act, or by striking with the evil eye, for the eye of the envier is deadly. But when he does not carry out his envy and does not act according to its requirement, his evil is weak. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three things no one escapes: envy, suspicion, and omen-taking." The way out of envy is that it should not remain; the way out of suspicion is that it should not be acted upon; the way out of omen-taking is that one should not turn back. Therefore he restricted it with his words "when he envies." If it is asked: the saying "from the evil of what He has created" is general and includes everything mentioned after it, so why was what follows mentioned? The answer: this is specification after generality, to give attention to what is mentioned after the general term. What is mentioned in this surah was emphasised after the generality because of the magic with which the Jews bewitched the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the intensity of their envy of him.

"If they envy me, I do not blame them, for before me the people of virtue were envied too,
So may there remain for me and for them what is with me and with them, and may most of us die of the rage at what he finds."

Then the envier's enmity never ceases, and his appeasement is of no use; he is a wrongdoer who complains as if he were wronged. And how true is the one who said:

"Every enmity may hope to have its removal, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy."

And the wisest of poets said:

"And the most wrongful of God's creatures is one who spends the night envious
Of one who spends the night turning in his blessings."

Ibn Atiyya said: some of the skilled scholars said: this surah is five verses, and it is what people mean by their saying to an envier from whom one fears the evil eye: "The five on your eye." If it is asked: why was it qualified with "when it settles" and "when he envies", with "idha", which implies the restriction of some times? The answer: the evil of the envier and his harm only occur when he carries out his envy; then he harms by his speech, by his act, or by striking with the evil eye, for the eye of the envier is deadly. But when he does not carry out his envy and does not act according to its requirement, his evil is weak. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three things no one escapes: envy, suspicion, and omen-taking." The way out of envy is that it should not remain; the way out of suspicion is that it should not be acted upon; the way out of omen-taking is that one should not turn back. Therefore he restricted it with his words "when he envies." If it is asked: the saying "from the evil of what He has created" is general and includes everything mentioned after it, so why was what follows mentioned? The answer: this is specification after generality, to give attention to what is mentioned after the general term. What is mentioned in this surah was emphasised after the generality because of the magic with which the Jews bewitched the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the intensity of their envy of him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 113, verses 1–5:

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. The meaning of "a'udhu" (I seek refuge) has already been explained in the discussion of seeking refuge (al-ta'awwudh), and the meaning of "rabb" (Lord) in the languages and in al-Fatiha. As for "al-falaq" (the daybreak), there are three opinions. The first: it is the dawn, from the phrase "faliq al-isbah" (the cleaver of the morning). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). The second: it is everything that God cleaves, such as the earth splitting to bring forth plants, mountains splitting to release springs, clouds splitting to release rain, wombs splitting to bring forth offspring, grains and date-pits, and other things. The third: it is a pit in Hell. This has been related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾. This is general over all created beings, and their evil takes many forms, from which God protect us. "Ma" here may be a relative pronoun (mawsulah), a descriptive (mawsufah), or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. On this there are seven opinions. The first: it is the night when it grows dark, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿until the darkening of the night﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. This is the view of most scholars. The darkness of night is when the people of evil, among mankind and jinn, spread out, and for this reason it is said in the proverb: "The night is more concealing for mischief." The second: it is the moon. Al-Nasai related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: "O Aisha, seek refuge in God from the evil of this, for it is the darkness when it settles." Its settling here means its eclipse, because "waqab" in the speech of the Arabs means darkness and blackness, and also means entering; so the meaning is when it enters into eclipse or when it becomes dark by it. The third: it is the sun when it sets, and "al-waqub" on this meaning is darkness or entering. The fourth: the darkness is the day when it enters the night, which is close to the preceding. The fifth: the darkness is the setting of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and diseases and plague would rise up at it. It has been related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The star is the darkness," so it may be that he meant the Pleiades. The sixth: al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the darkness" is meant the black snake, and its "settling" is its striking. The seventh: it is Iblis, related by al-Suhayli.

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. "Al-nafth" resembles blowing without spittle and saliva, as said by Ibn Atiyya, while al-Zamakhshari said it is blowing with saliva. This "nafth" is a kind of magic: that one blows over knots tied in a thread or the like, over the name of the person bewitched, so that it harms him. Ibn Atiyya related that a trustworthy person told him that he saw, among some people in the desert of the Maghrib, a red thread in which knots had been tied over young camels, which prevented them from suckling their mothers; whenever a knot was untied, that young camel would run to its mother and suckle at once. Al-Zamakhshari said: in seeking refuge from "the blowers" there are three aspects: first, that one seeks refuge from the likes of their deed, which is magic, for those who practise it. Second, that one seeks refuge from their deceit of people and their temptation. Third, that one seeks refuge from the evil that befalls by their blowing. "Al-naffathat" is an intensive form, and the qualified noun is omitted; its estimate is: the women who blow, or the group who blow, or the souls that blow. The first is more correct, because it has been related that it refers to the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam the Jew, who were sorceresses; they and their father bewitched the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and tied for him eleven knots, so God sent down the two refuges, eleven verses corresponding to the number of knots, and God healed His Messenger (ﷺ). If it is asked: why was "the blowers" defined with the article (al-), while what precedes it, "darkness", and what follows it, "envier", were indefinite, although all are things sought refuge from? The answer: the blowers were defined to indicate generality, since every blower is evil, unlike the darkness and the envier, whose evil is in some cases but not others.

﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. Envy is a blameworthy disposition, by nature and by the law. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Envy devours good deeds as fire devours firewood." Some scholars said: envy was the first sin by which God was disobeyed in heaven and on earth. In heaven, it was the envy of Iblis toward Adam; on earth, it was the killing of Hābīl by his brother Qābīl because of envy. Then envy has degrees. The first: that a person loves the removal of a blessing from his Muslim brother, even if it would not pass to him, rather he dislikes God's bounty upon another and is pained by it. The second: that he loves the removal of that blessing because he desires it and its transfer to himself. The third: that he wishes for himself the like of that blessing without loving its removal from others; this is permissible and is not envy, but rather is "ghibta" (emulation). The envier harms himself in three ways. First: the acquisition of sins, because envy is forbidden. Second: bad manners with God the Exalted, for the reality of envy is hatred of God's bestowal upon His servant and an objection to God in His action. Third: the heart's pain from its constant worry and grief. So we ask God to make us envied, not envious, for the envied is in blessing and the envier is in distress and affliction. And how well the one who said:

"Indeed I pity my envious ones, for the excess of what their breasts hold of rancour,
They look at God's dealings with me, so their eyes are in Paradise while their hearts are in Fire."

Another said:

"If they envy me, I do not blame them, for before me the people of virtue were envied too,
